sections.heading: Abstract
sections.text:
Electrochemical CO2 reduction with rationally designed copper-based electrocatalysts is a promising approach to reduce CO2 emission and produce valueadded products. Grain boundaries and micron-strains inside catalysts have been proposed as active catalytic sites, while the controlled formation of these sites has remained highly challenging. In this work, we developed a strategy of creating highdensity grain boundaries and micron-strains inside CuO electrocatalysts by fast cooling with liquid nitrogen. Compared to samples with slower cooling rates, the fast cooled CuO showed clear difference in their crystal domain sizes, micro-strain densities, and the chemisorption capacities of CO2 and CO. This micro-strain-rich CuO electrocatalyst exhibited a high total current density over 300 mA·cm-2, and an outstanding Faradaic efficiency for C2 products up to 78% (with a majority to ethanol) at −1.0 V vs. reversible hydrogen electrode. Our work suggests a facile approach of tuning grain boundaries and micro-strains inside Cu-based electrocatalysts to scale up electrochemical CO2 reduction for high value-added products. Keywords: CO2 reduction; electrocatalyst; micro-strain; grain boundaries; Faradaic efficiency

sections.heading: 1. Introduction
sections.text:
The growth rate of carbon dioxide (CO2) content has been accelerating in the past several decades.1 This accumulated CO2 level poses a great threat to the survival of humans and natural organisms. Aiming to maintain the neutral carbon cycle in the nature, a variety of carbon storage and conversion approaches have been investigated. Among them, the electrochemical CO2 reduction (ECR) features a mild working environment under ambient temperature and pressure. It utilizes electricity to reduce CO2 into carbon-containing molecules, such as carbon monoxide, hydrocarbons, and alcohols.2, 3 Among different electrocatalysts studied for ECR, Cu-based materials are a unique group of catalysts, with good electrical conductivity, low-cost, and capability of obtaining deep reduction (> 2-electron transfer) products,4-6 such as ethylene,7-9 ethanol10-12 and propanol.13 In particular, oxide-derived Cu (OD-Cu) based electrocatalysts have been demonstrated with high selectivities for C2+ products.14-16 A large number of grain boundaries (GBs) formed in the OD-Cu contribute to the high ECR performances.17 It was also reported that the annealing of GB-containing Cu catalysts could reduce the density of GBs,18 which was ascribed to the elimination of high-energy defect sites and growth of crystal domain size during thermal annealing. Similarly, copper oxides (CuOx) were also shown to be chemically engineered to present product-specific reactive sites during the oxide-derived process,19 which could be heritaged toward the reduced Cu catalysts. As an important catalyst feature, GBs can create strained regions in polycrystalline materials by stabilizing dislocations, which may enable high-energy surfaces for catalysis.18, 20-22 However, the capability of producing and well controlling GBs and micro-strains inside crystals has still remained significantly challenging.23, 24 On the other hand, the micro-strains are a kind of residual strains that are often formed in both crystals and amorphous materials such as glass, due to the over-fast temperature change. Indeed, different cooling rate can result in different physical properties of microcrystalline, which was conventionally studied in the glass manufacturing industry
4 and metal processing.25, 26 Inspired by this micro-strain formation mechanism, we proposed that a fast cooling strategy can also be leveraged to create GBs and micro-strains for ECR electrocatalysts. In this work, we demonstrate a fast cooling approach of high-temperture CuO nanoparticles (NPs) that can induce the formation of abundant GBs and micro-strains (Figure 1a), which are beneficial for enrichment of surface catalytic sites for ECR, especially for the C−C coupling steps (Figure 1b). As a proof-of-concept, CuO NPs prepared via the fast cooling method with liquid N2 presented significantly higher micron-strains than those prepared using water cooling or hot air cooling. The micronstrain-rich CuO NPs enabled a clearly increased selectivity of C2+ products, with an outstanding Faradaic efficiency (FE) of 78% at −1.0 V versus reversible hydrogen electrode (RHE).

sections.heading: 2. Materials and Methods
sections.text:
2.1 Chemical and materials Commercial copper powder (99.9% metals basis, 10−30 nm, Macklin). Potassium hydroxide (≥85.0%) and isopropanol (≥99.7) were purchased from the Sinopharm Chemical Reagent Company. Nafion solution (Dupont, D-521 dispersion, 5% w/w in water and 1-propanol). Freudenberg gas diffusion layer (GDL) was purchased from Fuel Cell Store. A hydroxide exchange membrane FAB-PK-130 was purchased from Fumatech and activated in 1.0 M NaCl aqueous for 12 hours. 2.2 Synthesis of CuO catalysts 1 g of Cu powder was placed into a porcelain boat and annealed in air for 2 hours at 500 oC, with a ramping rate at 10 oC·min-1. Afterwards, the porcelain boat was further treated by different methods. The porcelain was kept in the oven without opening the door till the hot air in the muffin furnace cooled to ambient temperature. Due to the
5 sluggish heat diffusion stacked by the insulation materials, this sample had the slowest cooling rate. It was labelled CuO-SC. The porcelain was immediately taken out of the 500 oC and directly dip into water for 20 min. Then the mixture was filtrated under vacuum and dry under ambient temperature. It was labelled CuO-MC. The porcelain was immediately taken out of the 500 oC and directly dip into liquid nitrogen for 5 min and kept in the liquid nitrogen. It was labelled CuO-FC. 2.3 Synthesis of Cu catalysts The CuO powder was gained by oxidizing Cu powder at 500 oC for 2 hours under air condition, and naturally cooled by the hot air. Afterwards, the CuO powder was reduced in the tube furnace under 5% hydrogen atmosphere, at 200 oC for 2 hours. The Cu powder was then poured directly into liquid nitrogen for 5 min under the inert gas and kept in the liquid nitrogen. It was labelled Cu- FC. For Cu- SC, the Cu powder was kept in the tube furnace until the temperature cooling down.

sections.heading: 3. Results and Discussion
sections.text:
The micro-strains inside the catalysts were introduced by a facile, fast cooling approach. In brief, copper oxide (CuO) nanoparticles were first synthesized and annealed at a high temperature (500 oC), and then was cooled down at different rates under various cooling environments (Figure 1a). For the super-fast cooling rate, the CuO nanoparticles were cooled in liquid N2 (−196 oC) to obtain the target catalyst, named CuO-FC (where FC indicates fast cooling rate). For comparison, the CuO nanoparticles were also cooled down by water (i.e., medium cooling rate, designated as CuO-MC) or hot air (i.e., slow cooling rate, designated as CuO-SC). The crystalline phases of these obtained samples were first characterized by X-ray diffraction (XRD, Figure 2a). All the three samples presented sharp diffraction peaks that were characteristic for the crystal structure of monoclinic CuO (PDF: 89-5895). No clear
6 differences were observed in the peak positions. This result suggested that the different cooling treatments did not alter their phases or crystal structures. Scanning electron microscopy (SEM) images showed that all these CuO samples were composed of many interconnected irregularly nano-crystallines, with average sizes of ~ 50 nm (Figure 2b-d). Transmission electron microscopy (TEM) images exhibited similar nano-crystalline morphologies of these samples. However, a slight decrease of the particle size was observed with the increase of the cooling rate (Figure 2e-g, Figure S1). This slight reduction of particle size may be possibly ascribed to the fact that the fast cooling rate can limit the atomic transfer rate in the Ostwald Ripening process, and thus impede the material growth.27 In addition, many GBs were clearly observed in these small CuO nanoparticles. The CuO-FC sample presented a highest density of these GBs (as shown in red dashed box in Fig. 2g). As reported by previous literature,21 this high density of GBs was beneficial for transforming into a grainboundary-rich (GB-rich) Cu crystal structure during the subsequent electrochemical reduction of CuO. X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) was then conducted to further study the electronic structures of these samples. For the Cu 3d spectra (Figure 2h), the peaks at ca. 954.2 and 934.1 eV corresponded to the 3d3/2 and 3d5/2 of CuO.28 The three peaks of 962.3, 944.0 and 941.5 eV were assigned to the satellite signals of Cu2+.28 The O 1s spectrum can be de-convoluted into two distinct sub-peaks at 531.8 and 530.0 eV (Figure 2i), which were ascribed to the surface oxygen and lattice oxygen in CuO.29 The XPS results suggest that no clear electron transfer was observed between Cu and neighboring atoms.30 The atomic ratios between Cu and O elements in the three CuO samples were listed (Table S1). In addition, the ratios of the lattice oxygen and surface oxygen were 1.3, 1.33, and, 1.43, respectively (Table S2). The results indicated that no obvious oxygen vacancies existed, and were different from previous work of oxygen vacancies in TiO2.29, 31 This phenomenon difference can be attributed to the lower oxygen vacancy formation energy in TiO2.32 In addition, the lattice strains induced by alloying or lattice mismatch at epitaxial interfaces typically show an obvious shift of
7 the shell electron energy.33-35 However, the micro-strains are more associated with surface or bulk defects and thus do not present such a trend.36 To investigate the micro-strains by different cooling treatments, XRD collected using synchrotron light source (SXRD) was further conducted to measure these samples (Figure 3a-c). The two-theta XRD patterns derived from the SXRD results were displayed (Figure S2), and the plane distances were calculated by using Bragg equation 2dsinθ = nλ, which were consistent with the results of the aforementioned 2- dimensional XRD (Figure 2a). The data of the SXRD were analyzed using Williamson−Hall analysis.18, 21 The scatters corresponded to each peak of the CuO samples were displayed (Figure 3d). A linear fitting was obtained and attributed to the following correlation: Bcosθ = Kλ/D + 4e*sinθ, where D is the average crystallite size, λ is the wavelength, e is the non-uniform strain (micro-strain), and the Scherrer constant K = 1.18, 21 The slopes of the linear fitting represented the micro-strains, and the crystallite sizes were calculated from the intercepts. The linear fitting results were summarized (Figure 3e), which showed an increasing slope with the cooling rate increase. Thus, CuO-FC exhibited the largest micro-strains. Meanwhile, CuO-FC also presented the largest intercept of the linear fittings, indicating the smallest crystallite size. The detailed fitting results of these three CuO samples were summarized (Table S3). The average sizes of the CuO-SC, CuO-MC and CuO-FC nanoparticles were 40.5, 35.8 and 35.3 nm, respectively. The effect of tuning the micro-strains and GBs in the CuO catalysts on the ECR performance was then investigated. Due to the low solubility of CO2 in aqueous solutions, the conventional H-type electrochemical cell can only have limited activities.37 In addition, the longer mass transportation path made the lower overpotential reaction of HER easier.38 Thus, the flow-cell with gas-diffusion layer (GDL) and high alkaline (1 M KOH) were used instead. About 0.25 mg·cm-2 of CuO catalyst was loaded onto the GDL. Before the ECR measurement, all the three CuO catalysts were electrochemically reduced to form pure copper (Figure S3). TEM images show that all the Cu catalysts were homogeneously dispersed on the edge of
8 porous carbon (Figure S4). High-resolution TEM images show that there was little reconstruction of catalysts, with the GBs still being clearly observed. Different orientations of Cu (100) and (110) were observed (Figure S4d), suggesting that different crystallite domains co-existed to form micro-strains. The electrochemical performances of these samples were first investigated by measuring the cyclic voltammetry (CV) profiles. The results displayed characteristic peaks between −0.3 and 0.5 V vs. RHE (Figure S5). The positive potential could be attributed to the reduce reaction of Cu2+ to Cu,38 and the negative potential was the water splitting into the hydrogen. The ECR activity was then measured under different applied potentials between − 0.3 and −1.2 V (vs. RHE, with iR-correction). For CuOSC, CuO-MC and CuO-FC, different products selectivity distribution of each electrocatalyst were displayed versus the applied potential (Figure 4a-c). The comparison of different samples was conducted within the limited potential difference. It can be seen that the H2 formation was maintained low with the FEs of < 20%, partially attributed to the pH effect in a high alkaline electrolyte.38 For all these three catalysts, CO, C2H4 and C2H5OH were the main ECR products. The ECR total current densities were close to 300 mA cm-2 at about −1.0 V vs. RHE. The onset potentials of C2 products (C2H4 and C2H5OH) were relatively more negative than those of C1 products, as the C−C coupling process is generally more sluggish.40 The partial current densities of C2 products were 246.3 (for CuO-MC) and 240.8 mA·cm-2 (for CuO-FC). The densities were 1.31 and 1.29 times higher than that of CuO-SC (186.9 mA·cm-2). In addition, a clear difference of ethanol (C2H5OH) and ethylene (C2H4) was also observed. CuO-FC presented an FE as high as 35.7% for ethanol production with a partial current density of 127.2 mA·cm-2. In contrast, CuO-MC exhibited an FE of only 18.6% for ethanol production, but with a partial current density of 179.9 mA·cm-2 for producing ethylene (Table S4-S6). The Faradaic efficiencies (FEs) of the total C2 products of different samples were further plotted with the applied potentials (Figure 4d). When the potential was less negative than −0.6 V, CuO-SC possessed a relatively high FE of C2 products. This is
9 because more unsaturated Cu sites in the smaller particle sizes of Cu-MC and Cu-FC resulted in higher H2 production at this potential range.41 At more negative applied potentials when the thermodynamic energy became more dominating for C−C coupling, both CuO-MC and CuO-FC showed better selectivities for C2 products at this potential range. The ratios between C2 and C1 products were displayed to show this trend (Figure 4e). In spite that CuO-FC had similar partial current densities for C2 formation as those of CuO-MC, the CuO-FC sample presented the largest ratios between C2 and C1 products in most of the potentials. For example, at −0.8 V vs. RHE, the ratio between C2 and C1 products was 7.04 for CuO-FC, substantially exceeding that of CuO-MC (4.48) and CuO-SC (2.00). This clear increase of C2 product formation suggests that micro-strains induced by fast cooling rate can help to stabilize the main intermediate toward C2 production, that is, *CO,37 and thus the subsequent C−C coupling steps. Moreover, the ratios between ethanol and C2H4 products were further compared among these three catalysts (Figure 4f). It can be seen that CuO-FC presented the highest ratio between ethanol and C2H4, with a peak value of 1.4 at −0.85 V vs. RHE. As suggested by recent literatures,42, 43 the improvement of *CO adsorption can lead to a higher surface coverage of *CO intermediate, favoring the subsequent oxygenate formation toward ethanol. To confirm our findings, we conducted another set of experiments by first reduced the CuO nanoparticles into Cu at high temperature, followed by fast cooling (using liquid nitrogen) or slow cooling (using natural room temperature), designated as CuFC and Cu-SC, respectively. XRD and corresponding Williamson-Hall analysis also demonstrated a similar trend that the Cu-FC obtained from fast cooling showed a higher density of micro-strains (Figure S6). The electrochemical CO2 reduction measurement using these catalysts demonstrated results of increased C2 products by fast-cooling Cu catalyst (Figure S7), similar to those of aforementioned CuO ones. Simultaneously, CuO (800)-FC was obtained by the same treatment with CuO annealed at 800 oC, which showed no obvious performance enhancement compared to CuO-FC (Figure S8). It demonstrated that a higher annealing temperature led a reduction of active sites.18
10
The capability of these three CuO catalysts for adsorption of CO2 and CO
molecules were studied by the CO2 temperature programmed desorption (CO2-TPD) and CO-TPD, respectively. All of three samples were reduced in 5% H2/Ar before the TPD experiments. For the CO2-TPD measurement (Figure 5a), both the CuO-FC (red curve) and CuO-MC (blue curve) had similar CO2 adsorption amounts, which were substantially greater than that of CuO-SC (black curve). The CO-TPD measurement (Figure 5b), on the other hand, indicated the relationships of the CO chemisorption strength and micro-strains. The desorption of CuO-FC was located at 290.5 oC, which was 55 oC and 63 oC higher than that of CuO-MC and CuO-SC, respectively. This result indicated that CuO-FC had a further enhancement of the CO adsorption capability.24 As *CO is a key intermediate in the ECR process to form C2+ products, the larger CO adsorption capability by the CuO-FC sample suggests its higher potential to produce C2+ products. Compared to the OD-Cu produced by traditional thermal process,15, 30, 44 GBs induced by the fast cooling can be an effective means to transform the selectivity form ethylene to ethanol.
In order to confirm the attributes of the different ECR performances of these
samples, their electrochemical surface areas (ECSA) were calculated by measuring their double-layer capacitances in the range of −0.3 and −0.2 V vs. RHE (Figure S9). The ECSA values were calculated as 1.1, 1.93 and 1.74 for CuO-SC, CuO-MC and CuO-FC, respectively, which were similar. The possible difference in crystal planes of these samples was also evaluated by studying the electro-sorption of oxygen (OHad) of these samples. CV curves were conducted between −0.95 and 0.55 V (vs. RHE) in Arsaturated 1 M KOH with 20 mV·s-1 (Figure 5c). The CV curves of all samples featured three peaks between −0.4 and −0.55 V that were attributed to the *OH adsorption on the three crystalline orientations of (100), (110), and (111), suggesting that there was a similar distribution of crystal surfaces. The relative ratios of different crystal planes were calculated by integrating these peaks (Figure 5d and Figure S10), which showed little difference of these oxide-derived catalysts. Thus, the difference in their ECR performances was not attributed to their crystal plane orientations. Furthermore, all the
11
samples exhibited a reduction peak at about 0.2 V vs. RHE, which was attributed to the conversion of Cu2+ into Cu(0) species.39 A slight difference in the reduction peak centers was also observed, which could also be attributed to the difference of microstrains resulted from the cooling rates. An annealing process could help to eliminate the residual strain produced by the different cooling processes (Figure S11).

sections.heading: 4. Conclusion
sections.text:
In summary, we developed a fast cooling approach by liquid nitrogen to increase
the densities of grain boundaries and micro-strains inside CuO catalysts. The abundant grain boundaries and micro-strains led to higher adsorption capability of *CO intermediates during the electrochemical CO2 reduction process. The CuO-FC electrocatalyst exhibited an enhanced selectivity of C2 products, with a 35.7% of FE and a high current density of 127 mA·cm-2 for ethanol production. Our work suggests new designs of creating high-density grain boundaries and even size-gradient for a host of variety of metal-based catalysts.
